title: Distributed Systems Problems — a field guide
subtitle: 27 classic problems across beginner, intermediate and advanced tiers — the what, how & why, with the year each was named, its solutions, and real papers & links.

tiers.name: Beginner
tiers.blurb: Foundational failure modes every backend engineer hits — load, caching, queries, and the basics of reliability.

topics.name: The thundering herd problem
topics.premise: Occurs when a single event (a resource becoming available, a lock releasing, a connection opening) wakes up a large number of waiting processes/threads at once, even though only one can make progress. The rest wake, contend, fail, and go back to sleep — wasting CPU and scheduling. At scale the churn can degrade or stall the system, including the process that "wins".
topics.year: 1990s-era systems/networking folklore (no single coining year). Documented in The Jargon File; widely discussed in the Unix/Linux kernel community (e.g. the accept() wake-up debates).
topics.why: Many waiters block on the same synchronization primitive or resource. When the event fires, the kernel/runtime wakes ALL of them instead of one, so they all race for a resource only one can hold — producing a contention spike and wasted work.
solutions: Wake-one / exclusive wake
Kernel wakes a single waiter per event. Linux added EPOLLEXCLUSIVE to epoll() in kernel 4.5 (2016); Windows IOCP can wake one thread per event.
Serialized acceptance
One thread accepts work and dispatches it, rather than many threads blocking on the same accept().
Exponential backoff + jitter
When clients retry after a shared event, randomize timing so they don't all re-converge on the same instant.
Request coalescing / leader
Designate one worker to do the work while others wait for its result (closely related to the cache-stampede lock fix).
topics.papers: No single canonical academic paper — an OS/networking-practice term. Documented in The Jargon File (v4.4.7). The jitter remedy: Marc Brooker, "Exponential Backoff And Jitter", AWS Architecture Blog, 2015.
topics.takeaway: Wake one, not the whole herd — and when clients must retry, scatter them with jitter.
topics.deepDive:
The thundering herd problem occurs when a large number of waiters — threads, processes, or remote clients — are all released or triggered by a single event and then simultaneously contend for one resource. The classic OS-level version is many threads blocked on the same socket or condition variable: an incoming connection wakes all of them, the kernel scheduler runs them all, but only one can accept() the connection while the rest do work just to discover there is nothing to do and go back to sleep. The wasted context switches and CPU spikes can dwarf the useful work. The distributed-systems version is more dangerous: a shared dependency (a database, a coordination service, a leader) briefly stalls or restarts, and the instant it recovers, thousands of clients that were retrying or blocked all reconnect or re-issue requests in the same millisecond, immediately re-saturating it. Synchronization is the root cause — independent actors become phase-locked by a common trigger.

The key trade-off is between responsiveness and stability. Waking exactly one waiter (e.g. Linux EPOLLEXCLUSIVE, or a single accept-thread pattern) eliminates herd wakeups but can hurt latency or load balancing across cores. On the client side, aggressive immediate retries minimize recovery latency for a single client but maximize correlated load; backoff trades a little extra latency per client for dramatically lower aggregate pressure. The crucial subtlety is that exponential backoff ALONE does not break a herd — if everyone fails at t=0 and uses the same 1s, 2s, 4s schedule, they stay synchronized and just retry together at each interval. Jitter (randomizing the wait) is what de-phases the herd; AWS's 'full jitter' picks a random value in [0, backoff] so retries spread smoothly over time.

Worked example: 10,000 app servers each hold a connection to a metadata service. A 200ms network blip drops the connections. All 10,000 detect failure within the same window and reconnect at once. The metadata service, sized for a steady trickle of renewals, now sees a 10,000-request spike; latency climbs, renewals start timing out, the now-'unhealthy' servers retry even harder, and the service is pinned at high error rate even though the original network blip is long gone. This is exactly the shape of the September 2015 DynamoDB outage. The fix is to cap concurrent reconnects (token bucket / connection rate limiting), add randomized jitter to retry timing, and add backpressure so the dependency can shed load rather than collapse.

Common pitfalls: assuming backoff without jitter is enough; retrying on the client AND at every intermediate layer so a single user action multiplies into a retry amplification storm; health checks that all fire on the same schedule and themselves become a herd; and 'recovery' code paths (cache warmups, leader re-election, reconnect logic) that are never load-tested because they only run during incidents — precisely when the herd is largest.

caseStudies.title: Amazon DynamoDB (US-East) — metadata service collapse (2015)
caseStudies.body: On September 20, 2015 a brief network disruption caused a large number of DynamoDB storage servers to simultaneously request membership data from the metadata service. Requests had already grown heavier (larger membership lists from Global Secondary Index adoption), so the synchronized surge plus continued retries from the servers that failed their renewals pinned error rates near 55% and kept the metadata service overloaded long after the network blip ended — a textbook thundering herd plus retry storm. AWS broke the cycle by pausing metadata requests, adding capacity, and tuning timeouts; the lesson was to size recovery paths for correlated spikes and rate-limit reconnection.

caseStudies.title: AWS US-EAST-1 — networking congestion collapse (2021)
caseStudies.body: On December 7, 2021 an automated scaling event triggered a large surge of connection activity that overwhelmed internal networking devices in US-EAST-1. The congestion produced errors that caused clients to make even more connection attempts and retries, creating persistent congestion; a latent bug prevented the clients' normal backoff behavior from kicking in, so the herd never de-phased on its own. It took manual intervention to relieve the surge, illustrating that backoff/jitter is only protective if it actually engages under load.

mcqs.q: Why does exponential backoff WITHOUT jitter often fail to prevent a thundering herd after a shared dependency recovers?
options: Exponential backoff increases the retry rate over time
All clients failed at the same instant, so identical backoff schedules keep them phase-locked and they retry together at each interval
Backoff only works for OS thread wakeups, not network clients
Jitter is purely a latency optimization with no effect on load distribution
mcqs.explanation: If everyone starts from the same failure time and uses the same deterministic schedule, they stay synchronized and spike together at 1s, 2s, 4s, etc. Randomized jitter is what spreads retries out; backoff alone only changes how often the synchronized spikes occur.

mcqs.q: An OS-level server has 500 threads all blocked on accept() for the same listening socket. One connection arrives. What is the thundering herd symptom?
options: All 500 threads are woken, all but one fail to get the connection and return to sleep, wasting CPU on context switches
The connection is silently dropped because of the contention
Only the oldest thread is woken and the rest stay blocked, which is the bug
The socket buffer overflows and corrupts the connection
mcqs.explanation: The classic herd wakes every waiter for a single event; only one can accept() while the rest burn scheduler/CPU cycles for nothing. Mechanisms like EPOLLEXCLUSIVE or a single accept-thread wake just one waiter to avoid this.

mcqs.q: Given: a cache/metadata service recovers from a 1-second blip and immediately 20,000 clients reconnect, re-saturating it and causing renewed failures. Which mitigation most directly addresses the root cause?
options: Increase each client's request timeout so failed requests wait longer
Add randomized jitter to reconnect timing and cap the concurrent reconnect rate (e.g. token bucket) so load is spread and bounded
Have every client retry immediately to minimize recovery time
Disable health checks during the incident
mcqs.explanation: The root cause is correlated, unbounded reconnect load. Jitter de-phases clients and a concurrency/rate cap bounds the spike so the dependency can recover. Longer timeouts and immediate retries either prolong or worsen the herd.

mcqs.q: A user action triggers a request that is retried by the client, the API gateway, AND the service's internal RPC layer, each up to 3 times. During a partial outage, why is this especially dangerous?
options: It improves availability because more layers means more chances to succeed
Retries multiply across layers (retry amplification), so one user action can become dozens of backend requests and turn a small herd into a massive one
It only affects latency, never load
Internal retries are free because they stay inside the data center
mcqs.explanation: Retries at multiple layers compound multiplicatively (3x3x3), so a slow dependency gets hit with far more traffic exactly when it is least able to cope. Retries should generally happen at a single layer with a global budget.

mcqs.q: Why are recovery code paths (reconnect logic, cache warmups, leader re-election) a common source of thundering-herd outages?
options: They run constantly and are therefore over-optimized
They typically only execute during incidents, so they are rarely load-tested at the scale and synchronization they actually face when everything fails at once
They are written in slower languages
They bypass all retry logic by design
mcqs.explanation: Recovery paths are exercised precisely when the largest, most synchronized herd exists, yet they are seldom tested under that correlated load. Steady-state testing hides the problem because the herd only forms during failure.

topics.name: Cache stampede
topics.premise: Also called dog-piling or a cache miss storm. When a popular cached value expires under high load, many concurrent requests all miss the cache at the same moment and simultaneously try to recompute the same value. Instead of one expensive recomputation the system does thousands at once, often hammering the database — a form of cascading failure.
topics.year: Industry/ops term from the high-traffic web era of the mid-to-late 2000s (memcached-heavy architectures); no single coining date. First rigorous academic treatment: Vattani, Chierichetti & Lowenstein (2015).
topics.why: A hot key has a single expiry time. The moment it expires, every in-flight request sees a miss; none knows the others are already recomputing, so they all recompute redundantly. More traffic + longer recompute = wider window and more duplicate work.
solutions: Locking / request coalescing
On a miss, the first request takes a lock and recomputes while others wait or serve stale — only one recomputation happens.
Probabilistic early expiration (XFetch)
Each reader independently rolls a dice to refresh BEFORE the TTL expires, with probability rising as expiry nears, so refreshes are staggered.
External / async recomputation
A background process refreshes hot keys ahead of expiry, so user requests never trigger the recompute.
Serve-stale-while-revalidate
Return the slightly stale value immediately and refresh in the background.
topics.papers: Vattani, Chierichetti & Lowenstein, "Optimal Probabilistic Cache Stampede Prevention", PVLDB 8(8):886–897, 2015 (verified via DBLP + ACM DOI 10.14778/2757807.2757813). Also: Allspaw & Robbins, Web Operations, O'Reilly, 2010.
topics.takeaway: Don't let a hot key expire for everyone at once — coalesce the recompute or refresh it early and probabilistically.
topics.deepDive:
A cache stampede (also called dog-piling) is a specific, cache-flavored thundering herd: a hot key expires (or is evicted, or the cache restarts cold), and every concurrent request that was being served from that key now misses simultaneously and tries to recompute the same value at once. Because none of the requesters knows the others are doing identical work, the expensive backing operation — a slow query, an API call, a heavy render — is executed N times in parallel against the origin. Under high traffic this can instantly overload the database. Worse, it can become self-sustaining: if recomputation now takes longer than the request timeout, every attempt times out, nothing ever gets written back to cache, the hit rate stays at zero, and the system is stuck in congestion collapse even though nothing is fundamentally broken.

There are three standard families of mitigation, each with trade-offs. (1) Locking / request coalescing: on a miss, a single requester acquires a per-key lock and does the recompute while others wait, serve stale, or fail fast. This prevents the stampede almost completely but adds an extra write per miss and requires careful handling of the lock holder crashing (need a lock TTL) and races. (2) External / asynchronous recomputation: a background job refreshes the value before it expires, so reads (almost) never miss. This decouples refresh cost from request load but adds a component to operate and fits static, enumerable keys far better than highly dynamic ones. (3) Probabilistic early expiration (XFetch): each reader independently rolls a dice that, with rising probability as the TTL approaches, decides to refresh the value early — so a few requests refresh ahead of expiry and the rest keep using the still-valid cached value, staggering recomputes instead of cliff-edging them all at once. It is simple and needs no coordination but uses a little extra cache lifetime.

Worked example: a page costs 3 seconds to render and is requested 10 times per second; it is cached with a 60s TTL. For 60 seconds everything is a cheap cache hit. At the instant of expiry, the ~30 in-flight requests during that 3-second render window all miss together and all kick off the 3-second render against the database — 30 simultaneous heavy renders where 1 would have sufficed. With locking, the first request renders and the other 29 wait (or serve the just-expired value); with XFetch, a handful of requests would have quietly refreshed at, say, t=55–59s so the hard expiry never produces a synchronized miss.

Common pitfalls: setting identical TTLs on many related keys so they all expire on the same second (add TTL jitter); treating a cache flush/redeploy as safe when a cold cache means EVERY key stampedes at once; relying on a lock without a TTL so a crashed lock-holder blocks all readers forever; and forgetting negative caching, so a key that legitimately has no value misses and recomputes on every request. The 'never expire, refresh in background, serve stale on error' pattern is often the most robust because reads are decoupled from the volatile backing store entirely.

caseStudies.title: Facebook — memcache 'leases' to stop stampedes and stale sets (NSDI 2013)
caseStudies.body: Facebook's 'Scaling Memcache at Facebook' paper documents that highly popular keys caused thundering herds: when a hot key was invalidated, huge numbers of clients missed simultaneously and stampeded the databases to recompute it, and concurrent updates also produced stale sets. They engineered 'leases' — memcache hands a token to the first client that misses a key, that client is allowed to recompute and set the value, while other clients briefly wait and retry the cache. This is essentially request coalescing / single-flight at the cache tier and remains a canonical real-world fix for cache stampede at scale.

mcqs.q: What makes a cache stampede potentially self-sustaining (congestion collapse) rather than a brief spike?
options: The cache permanently deletes the key on the first miss
If parallel recomputes make each recompute slower than the request timeout, every attempt times out, nothing is ever written back, and the hit rate stays at zero
Caches cannot store recomputed values after an expiry
The database refuses all connections after one timeout
mcqs.explanation: When recompute latency exceeds the timeout, no result is ever cached, so misses never stop and the system stays pinned even after the original trigger. A brief spike becomes a stable failure mode.

mcqs.q: A team caches dozens of related keys, all set with exactly TTL=300s, populated together at deploy time. Why does this invite a stampede?
options: Long TTLs always cause stampedes
All those keys expire on the same second, so a synchronized wave of misses hits the origin simultaneously every 5 minutes
Related keys share memory and corrupt each other
TTLs under 600s are never honored by caches
mcqs.explanation: Identical TTLs created at the same moment create a synchronized expiry cliff. Adding random jitter to each TTL de-correlates expirations so misses spread out instead of arriving as one wave.

mcqs.q: Given a single extremely hot key (e.g. a homepage fragment) under very high QPS, which mitigation most directly prevents N parallel recomputes on expiry?
options: Increase the database connection pool size
Per-key locking / single-flight so only one request recomputes while others wait or serve stale, plus probabilistic early refresh
Lower the TTL so it expires more often
Remove the cache and read from the database every time
mcqs.explanation: Single-flight collapses N concurrent recomputes into one, which is exactly Facebook's 'leases' approach. Bigger pools just let more redundant work hit the DB, and a lower TTL makes stampedes more frequent.

mcqs.q: How does probabilistic early expiration (XFetch) avoid a stampede without any cross-request coordination?
options: It locks the key globally before every read
Each reader independently refreshes early with a probability that rises as the TTL nears, so a few refresh ahead of time while most still hit the valid cached value
It disables expiry entirely so values never need recomputing
It routes all reads to a dedicated recompute server
mcqs.explanation: XFetch staggers recomputes by having each request roll an independent, time-weighted dice, so the hard-expiry synchronized miss never happens — no lock or shared state required, at the cost of a little extra cache lifetime.

mcqs.q: After a Redis restart leaves the cache completely cold, traffic immediately overwhelms the database. Why is a cold cache a worst-case stampede, and what is the best immediate guard?
options: Cold caches are fine; the issue must be a network bug
Every key misses at once (not just one hot key), so coalescing/locking plus controlled cache warming and request rate-limiting are needed to bound origin load
Restarting Redis again will repopulate it instantly
Increasing the TTL retroactively repopulates expired keys
mcqs.explanation: A cold cache means the entire keyspace stampedes simultaneously, far worse than a single hot key. Single-flight per key plus deliberate warming and admission control bound how much of that load reaches the database.

topics.name: N+1 query problem
topics.premise: Occurs when fetching a list of N parent records and then issuing one more query per record to load related data — 1 query for the list plus N for the children, N+1 total. What should be one or two queries balloons into hundreds, and per-query round-trip latency dominates. Most common with ORMs and lazy loading.
topics.year: A software-engineering/database term from ORM practice, popularized in the early-to-mid 2000s as Hibernate/ActiveRecord went mainstream. No single founding paper or precise year.
topics.why: ORMs lazy-load associations by default. When you iterate a collection and touch each item's related object, the ORM transparently issues a fresh query for each one — the developer sees simple property access in a loop but the framework silently emits N round trips.
solutions: Eager loading
Tell the ORM to load associations up front (Django select_related/prefetch_related, Rails includes, Hibernate fetch joins).
JOIN fetch
Use a single SQL JOIN to pull parents and children together.
Batch / IN-clause loading
Collect the IDs and fetch all children with one WHERE id IN (...) query.
DataLoader / batching layer
In GraphQL stacks, a DataLoader coalesces per-item lookups within a tick into one batched query.
Bulk writes
For the write equivalent, use bulk insert/update instead of saving in a loop.
topics.papers: No formal academic paper — an ORM/industry-practice concept. Discussed in Martin Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture, Addison-Wesley, 2002 (lazy-load / data-access context).
topics.takeaway: If you're querying inside a loop, you're probably doing N+1 — fetch the related data in one batched or joined query instead.
topics.deepDive:
The N+1 query problem is a data-access anti-pattern, most famous in ORMs but present in any code that fetches a collection and then lazily fetches a related entity per element. You run 1 query to load a list of N parent rows, then, as your code touches a related field on each parent, the ORM silently issues 1 additional query per parent to load that relation — for a total of N+1 round trips. The damage is rarely CPU; it is latency and connection pressure from round trips. Even if each child query is a fast indexed lookup of, say, 1ms, doing 1,000 of them serially adds ~1 second of pure network/latency overhead, and it scales linearly with result-set size, so it behaves fine on a developer's 10-row test database and falls over in production at 10,000 rows.

The core mechanism is lazy loading: the ORM defers loading a relationship until it is accessed, which is ergonomic but hides the cost behind an innocent-looking property access inside a loop. The standard fixes trade round trips for a bit more query complexity or memory. (1) Eager loading via a JOIN ('include'/'joinedload'/'includes' in a single query) collapses N+1 into 1 query but can multiply rows and inflate payload for one-to-many relations (the Cartesian explosion). (2) Batched/IN-clause loading ('preload', 'selectinload', DataLoader-style batching) turns N+1 into exactly 2 queries: one for parents, one 'WHERE child.parent_id IN (...)' for all children — usually the best balance because it avoids row multiplication. (3) Projection — only select the columns you actually need so the relation isn't triggered at all.

Worked example: rendering a list of 100 blog posts, each showing its author's name. Naively: 'SELECT * FROM posts LIMIT 100' (1 query), then for each post 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?' (100 queries) = 101 queries. With a JOIN: 'SELECT posts.*, users.name FROM posts JOIN users ...' = 1 query. With batching: load 100 posts, collect their author_ids, then 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE id IN (...)' = 2 queries. In GraphQL this is endemic because resolvers run per-node; the conventional fix is the DataLoader pattern, which coalesces per-field lookups within a tick into a single batched query.

Common pitfalls: 'fixing' N+1 with a JOIN on a one-to-many relation and accidentally multiplying parent rows (then deduping in app code, which wastes bandwidth) — batching is usually better there; nested N+1, where eager-loading one level still leaves a lazy second level (post -> comments eager, but comment -> author lazy); caching masking the problem in tests so it only appears under cache misses; and the inverse over-fetching trap, where blanket eager-loading every relation pulls huge unused payloads. The reliable workflow is to log/inspect the actual SQL count per request (or use query-count assertions / tools like the 'bullet' gem) so N+1 regressions are caught before production.

mcqs.q: Why does an N+1 query problem often pass code review and tests but cause an incident in production?
options: It only occurs on weekends
Round trips scale linearly with result-set size, so a 10-row dev dataset looks fast while a 10,000-row production dataset issues 10,001 queries
ORMs disable it in test mode
Production databases are slower per query by design
mcqs.explanation: The cost is proportional to N, which is tiny in dev fixtures and large in production. The per-query latency might be fine; it is the sheer count of serial round trips that kills you at scale.

mcqs.q: An endpoint loads 500 orders and, for each, lazily accesses 'order.customer'. Which fix turns this into a constant 2 queries without risking row multiplication?
options: A JOIN between orders and customers
Batched loading: collect the customer_ids and issue one 'SELECT ... WHERE id IN (...)'
Increase the connection pool size
Add a per-customer cache with a 1s TTL
mcqs.explanation: Batched/IN-clause loading produces exactly two queries and avoids the Cartesian row inflation a one-to-many JOIN can cause. A JOIN here is many-to-one so it is safe, but batching is the general, multiplication-free answer.

mcqs.q: A developer fixes an N+1 by eager-loading a one-to-many relation (posts with their many comments) using a single JOIN. What new problem can this introduce?
options: It will always return wrong results
Row multiplication: each post row is duplicated once per comment, inflating the result set and bandwidth, requiring app-side de-duplication
It permanently locks the comments table
It converts the query into N+1 again automatically
mcqs.explanation: JOINing a one-to-many fans out parent rows by the number of children (Cartesian explosion), wasting bandwidth and memory. A separate batched query ('selectinload'/'preload') avoids the multiplication.

mcqs.q: In a GraphQL API, a list field resolver triggers one database lookup per item for a nested field. Which pattern is the conventional fix?
options: Disable nested fields in the schema
The DataLoader pattern, which coalesces the per-item lookups within a tick into a single batched query
Add a longer HTTP timeout
Return the list unsorted
mcqs.explanation: GraphQL resolvers run per node, so naive resolvers are inherently N+1; DataLoader batches and caches the per-key loads within an execution tick into one query. Timeouts and schema changes do not address the query count.

mcqs.q: After eager-loading 'post.comments', an endpoint is still slow and the SQL log shows hundreds of queries. What is the most likely cause?
options: Eager loading never works
Nested N+1: comments were eager-loaded but each comment still lazily loads 'comment.author', so the second level is still N+1
The database index was dropped
The ORM cache is too large
mcqs.explanation: Fixing one relationship level leaves deeper relationships lazy, so the N+1 just moves down a level. You must eager/batch-load the full access path (e.g. comments AND their authors).

topics.name: Hot partition / hot key
topics.premise: In a partitioned/sharded datastore, a disproportionate share of reads or writes targets a single partition key or physical partition. Because each partition has its own throughput ceiling, that one partition saturates and throttles while the rest of the cluster sits idle — the system is far below aggregate capacity yet still errors on the hot key.
topics.year: A distributed-database/partitioning term from ops practice; prominent with horizontally partitioned NoSQL systems of the late 2000s–2010s (DynamoDB, Cassandra, HBase, Kafka). No single coining year.
topics.why: Throughput is provisioned per partition, but data maps to partitions by hashing/ranging the key. A skewed access pattern — low-cardinality key, celebrity/viral item, monotonically increasing key (timestamps, sequential IDs) — concentrates traffic onto one key/partition, so that partition's per-partition limit becomes the bottleneck (e.g. DynamoDB ~3,000 RCU / 1,000 WCU per partition).
solutions: Write sharding (random suffix)
Append a random number (key.1…key.200) to spread writes; reads query all suffixes and merge.
Write sharding (calculated suffix)
Derive the suffix deterministically from a queryable attribute so you can spread writes and still read a specific item directly.
High-cardinality partition key
Avoid low-cardinality and monotonically increasing keys so load spreads evenly.
Adaptive capacity
Some systems (DynamoDB) automatically shift capacity toward hot partitions, smoothing transient skew.
Cache the hot key
Put a cache (DAX, Redis) in front to absorb reads on a celebrity key before it reaches the partition.
topics.papers: No single canonical paper. Closely related foundation: DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store", SOSP 2007 (consistent hashing & partitioning). Primary practical guidance: AWS DynamoDB partition-key best-practices docs.
topics.takeaway: Throughput limits are per partition, so a skewed key bottlenecks one shard — spread the load with sharding or a better-distributed key.
topics.deepDive:
A hot partition (or hot key / hot shard) occurs when a sharded data store distributes data evenly by key space but the actual access pattern is heavily skewed toward one key or one narrow range. Even though the dataset is spread across many physical partitions, the bulk of read/write traffic lands on a single partition. That partition's owning node saturates its CPU, IOPS, or per-partition throughput cap while the rest of the fleet sits nearly idle. The cluster's aggregate capacity is large, but capacity is not fungible across partitions, so the system throttles or errors despite being mostly empty of work elsewhere. This is fundamentally an imbalance problem, not a total-capacity problem.

The mechanism is rooted in how the partition key maps to placement. With consistent hashing or range partitioning, key K always resolves to the same partition. If K is a celebrity user id, a viral tweet, a 'global counter' row, or a low-cardinality value like country='US', every request for that value funnels to one place. DynamoDB, Cassandra, and Kafka all expose this: a Kafka topic partitioned by a key with one dominant value sends all those records to one partition/consumer; a relational table sharded by tenant_id breaks when one tenant is 100x larger than the rest.

Worked example: an e-commerce site shards a 'product_views' table by product_id across 50 shards. Normally each shard handles ~2,000 writes/sec, well under its 10,000/sec cap. A flash sale on one SKU drives 80,000 views/sec to that single product_id. All 80,000 hit one shard, which caps at 10,000/sec; ~70,000 writes/sec are throttled or dropped while the other 49 shards idle. Aggregate cluster capacity (500,000/sec) is irrelevant because the work cannot be redistributed by key.

Fixes and trade-offs: (1) Key salting / write sharding — append a random suffix (product_id#0..N) to spread writes across N sub-partitions, then scatter-gather on read; trade-off is read amplification and loss of single-key atomicity. (2) Caching / request coalescing in front of the hot key absorbs reads but not writes. (3) Adaptive capacity / partition splitting (DynamoDB does this automatically, but with lag). (4) Choosing a higher-cardinality, well-distributed partition key up front. Common pitfalls: using monotonically increasing keys (timestamps, auto-increment ids) which create a 'hot tail' partition; assuming a uniform hash guarantees uniform load (it only balances key space, not request volume); and adding capacity to the whole cluster, which does nothing because the bottleneck is one partition.

caseStudies.title: AWS DynamoDB — GSI partitions overload one metadata service (2015)
caseStudies.body: On September 20, 2015 in US-East-1, rapid adoption of Global Secondary Indexes inflated storage servers' partition membership lists. Because GSIs add their own partitions, a small number of large tables concentrated disproportionate metadata-processing load, pushing the metadata service past its time budget for serving membership lookups. While the full event became a retry storm, the underlying trigger was a skewed, oversized partition set on a constrained subsystem. AWS's fix included increasing metadata capacity and later segmenting the metadata service into many instances each serving only a portion of the fleet — reducing the blast radius of any single hot region of the key space.

mcqs.q: A Kafka topic is partitioned by customer_id. One enterprise customer generates 90% of all events. What symptom do you expect?
options: All partitions fill evenly because Kafka hashes keys uniformly
One partition and its single consumer lag heavily while others stay nearly empty
The producer automatically rebalances the load across partitions
Total cluster throughput drops to zero
mcqs.explanation: Hashing distributes the key space evenly, not request volume. A dominant key value always maps to the same partition, so that one partition (and the consumer assigned to it) saturates and lags while the rest idle.

mcqs.q: Your DynamoDB table is throttling writes, but CloudWatch shows total consumed capacity far below the provisioned table capacity. What is the most likely cause?
options: The table needs more total provisioned capacity
A hot partition is exceeding its per-partition throughput limit
DynamoDB is in a maintenance window
The SDK retry count is set too low
mcqs.explanation: Provisioned capacity is divided across partitions. If traffic concentrates on one partition key, that partition hits its per-partition cap and throttles even though table-wide consumption looks low. Adding total capacity does not fix the imbalance.

mcqs.q: Which partition key choice is MOST likely to create a hot partition?
options: A high-cardinality UUID per item
A hash of (user_id, session_id)
A monotonically increasing timestamp truncated to the current day
A randomly salted composite key
mcqs.explanation: A timestamp truncated to 'today' means every current write shares the same key value, funneling all live traffic into one partition (a 'hot tail'). High-cardinality and salted keys spread load.

mcqs.q: A read-heavy hot key (a viral post) is overloading one shard. Which mitigation best targets reads specifically?
options: Salting the write key into N sub-partitions
Putting a cache or request-coalescing layer in front of that key
Increasing the cluster's total node count
Switching from range to hash partitioning
mcqs.explanation: For a read hotspot, a cache or request coalescing absorbs repeated reads of the same value without touching the shard. Write salting helps writes, not reads; adding nodes does not redistribute a single key's load.

mcqs.q: After salting a hot write key into product_id#0..#15, what new cost is introduced on the read path?
options: Reads now require a scatter-gather across all 16 sub-partitions and aggregation
Reads become impossible without a full table scan
Reads bypass the cache entirely
Reads lose strong consistency for unrelated keys
mcqs.explanation: Salting spreads writes but fragments a logical key across many physical partitions, so a complete read must query all sub-partitions and merge results (read amplification) — the main trade-off of write sharding.

topics.name: Single point of failure (SPOF)
topics.premise: Any one component whose failure takes down the entire system, because no redundant alternative exists. If the box, link, process, or person it represents stops, everything depending on it stops too. Eliminating SPOFs is the foundation of designing for high availability.
topics.year: A foundational reliability-engineering concept with no single coining event; dates to mid-20th-century systems engineering and the survivable-network work behind packet switching (Paul Baran, Donald Davies, 1960s). Treat it as a 1960s–70s era term.
topics.why: A single instance of a critical resource sits on the request path with no backup — one DB primary, one load balancer, one network link, one config server, even one human with sole access. Any unreplicated dependency on the critical path is a latent SPOF.
solutions: Redundancy / N+1
Run two or more interchangeable instances so one can fail without downtime.
Failover + health checks
Detect a dead component and route to a standby (active-passive) or surviving peers (active-active).
Geographic distribution
Spread replicas across availability zones/regions so a site-level failure isn't fatal.
Load balancing
Front a pool of identical nodes so traffic shifts off failed members automatically.
Quorum/replication for state
Replicate data across nodes (majority quorum) so no single copy is load-bearing.
Eliminate hidden SPOFs
Audit shared dependencies (DNS, a single NAT gateway, one cert authority, one deploy key) that app-tier redundancy doesn't cover.
topics.papers: No single formal paper defines the term — core reliability practice. Lineage: Baran, "On Distributed Communications" (RAND, 1964). Treatments in Beyer et al., Site Reliability Engineering (O'Reilly, 2016).
topics.takeaway: If one part can take down the whole system, you don't have a system — you have a liability with a hostname.
topics.deepDive:
A single point of failure (SPOF) is any component whose failure takes down the entire system because there is no redundant path around it. The defining property is a multiplicative dependency: if availability of the whole system equals the product of the availabilities of components on the critical path, then any non-redundant component caps the system at its own availability. A 99.9% load balancer in front of a perfectly redundant backend still limits the service to 99.9%. SPOFs hide not only in obvious infrastructure (a single database primary, one load balancer, one NAT gateway) but in control-plane and naming dependencies that are easy to overlook — DNS, certificate authorities, authentication/identity services, configuration stores, and service discovery.

The trade-off is cost and complexity versus blast radius. Eliminating a SPOF means adding redundancy (active-active or active-passive), which introduces its own problems: state replication, split-brain risk, failover detection latency, and the danger that the failover mechanism itself becomes a SPOF. A classic mistake is making the data plane redundant while leaving the control plane (the thing that performs failover, health checks, or DNS updates) single-homed. The most damaging real outages are often control-plane or dependency SPOFs, not server crashes — because they disable the very tools needed to recover.

Worked example: a service runs three stateless app servers behind one load balancer, all in one availability zone, all reading config from one central config service at startup. Engineers believe they have 3x redundancy. In reality there are at least three SPOFs: the single load balancer (no path around it), the single AZ (a power/network event drops all three servers at once), and the config service (if it is down during a deploy or restart, no server can boot). True redundancy means multi-AZ placement, redundant or DNS-based load balancing, and config that is cached locally so a dependency outage does not block startup.

Common pitfalls and lessons: (1) Self-referential dependencies — the AWS S3 2017 outage took down the Service Health Dashboard because the dashboard itself depended on S3, so AWS could not even report the outage. (2) Health-signal SPOFs — Facebook's 2021 outage withdrew DNS routes because the DNS servers were designed to self-withdraw when they lost backbone connectivity, turning a backbone fault into a total namelookup blackout. (3) 'Hidden' shared fate — components that look independent but share a rack, power feed, AZ, deployment pipeline, or a common dependency like an auth service. The remedy is to map the full critical path including control-plane and naming dependencies, then ask for each node: 'if this dies, does the system survive?'

caseStudies.title: AWS S3 — fat-finger removes index servers, dashboard self-dependency (2017)
caseStudies.body: On February 28, 2017 in US-EAST-1, an engineer running a debugging playbook mistyped a command and removed far more capacity than intended, taking out servers backing the S3 index and placement subsystems, which had to be fully restarted. Because countless services (EC2 launches, EBS, Lambda) and even AWS's own Service Health Dashboard depended on S3 in that region, S3 was effectively a SPOF whose failure cascaded broadly — AWS could not even update its dashboard and resorted to Twitter. Fixes included slowing the capacity-removal tool, adding safety floors, partitioning the index subsystem into smaller cells to shrink blast radius, and running the health dashboard across multiple regions.

caseStudies.title: Facebook/Meta — BGP withdrawal makes DNS unreachable (2021)
caseStudies.body: On October 4, 2021, a maintenance command intended to assess backbone capacity accidentally disconnected Meta's data centers from the global backbone, and an audit tool that should have blocked it had a bug. Meta's DNS servers are designed to withdraw their BGP route advertisements whenever they lose data-center connectivity; with the backbone gone they all self-withdrew, so the entire facebook.com/Instagram/WhatsApp namespace became unresolvable worldwide. The health-signal mechanism acted as a SPOF: a backbone fault turned into a total naming blackout, and the same failure disabled internal tools, forcing physical on-site recovery. Lessons centered on better audit-tool safeguards and simulating full backbone-loss scenarios.

caseStudies.title: AWS US-EAST-1 — internal network as a hidden control-plane SPOF (2021)
caseStudies.body: On December 7, 2021, an automated scaling activity triggered a surge of connections that congested the devices bridging AWS's internal network to the main network. That internal network hosts foundational dependencies — internal DNS, monitoring, authorization, and parts of the EC2 control plane — so its impairment broke EC2 APIs, Route 53 APIs, STS/Console logins, and CloudWatch across the region, even though many data planes (running instances, existing DNS answers) stayed up. The internal network was a shared control-plane SPOF, and its failure also blinded operators by killing real-time monitoring. AWS deployed network configuration to protect the bridging devices and disabled the triggering scaling activity.

mcqs.q: A service has three redundant app servers but they all sit behind one load balancer in one availability zone. How many SPOFs are present?
options: Zero — three servers means full redundancy
Only the load balancer
At least two — the single load balancer and the single AZ
Only the availability zone
mcqs.explanation: The single load balancer is a non-redundant path to all three servers, and the single AZ means one power/network event drops all of them together. Server count does not help when upstream and placement are single-homed.

mcqs.q: Why did the AWS S3 2017 outage prevent AWS from updating its own Service Health Dashboard?
options: The dashboard was under DDoS attack
The dashboard itself depended on S3, a self-referential SPOF
Engineers forgot the dashboard password
The dashboard was being deployed at the time
mcqs.explanation: The dashboard relied on the very S3 service that was down, so the SPOF disabled the recovery/communication tooling too. AWS later moved the dashboard to run across multiple regions.

mcqs.q: In the Facebook 2021 outage, why did a backbone disconnection escalate into a total DNS blackout?
options: The DNS servers crashed from overload
DNS servers were designed to withdraw their BGP routes when they lost data-center connectivity, so they removed themselves from the internet
An attacker hijacked the BGP routes
The DNS cache TTLs expired simultaneously
mcqs.explanation: The health-signal logic (self-withdraw BGP on connectivity loss) turned a backbone fault into a naming SPOF: the still-functioning DNS servers became unreachable because they pulled their own routes.

mcqs.q: Your team makes the database tier active-active across two regions but the automated failover controller runs on a single host. What is the risk?
options: No risk — the data tier is fully redundant
The failover controller is now a SPOF; if it dies during an incident, failover cannot occur
Active-active databases cannot have a controller
The two regions will always split-brain
mcqs.explanation: Redundant data plane with a single-homed control plane is a classic mistake. The mechanism that performs failover must itself be redundant, or it becomes the new SPOF exactly when you need it most.

mcqs.q: Which dependency is the LEAST obvious but still a common SPOF that can prevent a service from even starting up?
options: A second redundant web server
A central config/secrets service that every instance must reach at boot
A local in-memory cache
A read replica used only for analytics
mcqs.explanation: If every instance must fetch config or secrets from one central service at startup, that service is a hidden SPOF: when it is down during a deploy or mass restart, nothing can boot. Caching config locally removes the hard dependency.

topics.name: Retry storm
topics.premise: Many clients (or many layers of a call stack) react to a slow or failing dependency by retrying at once, multiplying load on the already-struggling service and preventing recovery. Because each layer can retry independently, load multiplies layer-by-layer ("retry amplification"), producing a self-sustaining overload that often outlasts the original trigger.
topics.year: The underlying thundering-herd effect was in 1990s systems literature; the "retry storm"/"retry amplification" framing is industry vocabulary popularized through the 2010s by cloud teams (AWS, Azure). Azure formally documents it as the "Retry Storm antipattern".
topics.why: Naive retry logic (immediate retries, fixed intervals, unbounded counts, retries at every layer) converts one failed request into a flood. A 5-deep stack with 3 retries per layer can multiply downstream load by up to 3^5 = 243×.
solutions: Exponential backoff
Wait progressively longer between attempts so clients stop hammering a struggling service.
Jitter
Add randomness so retries don't synchronize into clustered waves.
Capped retries / time budgets
Stop after a few attempts or a short window — old requests are usually stale anyway.
Retry at a single layer
Retry at one point (e.g. the edge) instead of every layer, to prevent multiplication.
Token-bucket retry budgets
Limit retries to a small fraction of total requests (added to AWS SDK in 2016).
Circuit breakers
Trip open after repeated failures so calls fail fast instead of retrying into the void.
Honor Retry-After
Respect server signals (HTTP 429/503 + Retry-After) rather than retrying blindly.
topics.papers: No formal academic paper — industry practice. Canonical: Marc Brooker, "Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter", Amazon Builders' Library; and "Exponential Backoff And Jitter" (AWS Architecture Blog, 2015).
links: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter — AWS
topics.takeaway: Retries are selfish — without backoff, jitter, and budgets, a thousand polite clients become a denial-of-service attack on the service they're trying to reach.
topics.deepDive:
A retry storm (a form of metastable failure / congestion collapse) happens when many clients respond to errors or latency by retrying, and the aggregate retry traffic itself becomes the load that keeps the system overloaded. A transient trigger — a brief network blip, a small latency spike, a partial dependency failure — causes some requests to fail. Each client retries, often immediately and multiple times, so offered load jumps to 2x–5x the original. That surplus traffic pushes the server further past capacity, causing more failures, which generate still more retries. The system locks into a stable but broken equilibrium that persists even after the original trigger is long gone, because retries are now self-sustaining the overload.

The mechanism hinges on retries amplifying load precisely when the system is least able to absorb it. Naive fixed retries with no jitter cause synchronized retry waves (the 'thundering herd'): all clients that failed at T retry at T+1s together. Layered retries multiply catastrophically — if a gateway retries 3x, a service it calls retries 3x, and that service's DB client retries 3x, a single user request can become 27 backend calls. The defenses are: exponential backoff with full jitter (spread retries over a widening, randomized window), a retry budget / token bucket that caps retries to a small fraction (e.g. 10%) of total traffic, circuit breakers that fail fast and stop sending traffic to an unhealthy dependency, and load shedding so an overloaded server rejects excess work cheaply instead of collapsing.

Worked example: a service handles 10,000 rps at 99.9% success. A 2-second network blip causes a burst of failures. With a fixed 'retry up to 3 times immediately' policy and no jitter, those failed requests plus their retries spike offered load to ~30,000 rps. The server, sized for 10,000, now times out broadly, so nearly every request fails and retries — load stays pinned near 30,000 rps and success stays near 0% even after the network recovers. The only escape is to reduce load: clients must back off, or the server must shed load. With exponential backoff + full jitter + a 10% retry budget, the same blip produces a small, spread-out bump that the server absorbs, and it self-heals.

Common pitfalls: retrying non-idempotent or non-retryable errors (4xx, validation failures) which can never succeed and just waste capacity; retrying at multiple layers without a shared budget; backoff without jitter (synchronized herds); and no way to recover except a full restart because the system cannot exit the bad equilibrium on its own. The deep lesson: retries are a client-side decision with system-wide consequences. Safe retry policy means cap the count, add full jitter, scope a global budget, fail fast with circuit breakers, and shed load on the server so the system has a path back to a healthy state.

caseStudies.title: AWS DynamoDB — metadata service retry storm (2015)
caseStudies.body: On September 20, 2015 in US-East-1, a brief network disruption caused many storage servers to simultaneously re-request partition membership data from a metadata service already strained by oversized membership lists. Servers that failed their membership renewal removed themselves and kept retrying, which kept the metadata service under heavy load and slowed responses even for healthy servers, dragging them down too — a self-sustaining feedback loop that drove DynamoDB error rates to about 55%. Attempts to add capacity failed because retry load saturated the service; recovery only came at 5:06am PDT when AWS deliberately paused metadata requests, cutting retries so capacity could be added and traffic safely re-enabled. Fixes included more metadata capacity, monitoring on membership size, and later segmenting the metadata service per fleet portion.

caseStudies.title: AWS US-EAST-1 — congestion collapse from failed back-off (2021)
caseStudies.body: On December 7, 2021, an automated scaling activity triggered a large surge of connections from internal-network clients to the devices bridging AWS's internal and main networks. The surge caused latency and errors, which drove even more connection attempts and retries; a latent bug prevented these clients from adequately backing off, so the retries sustained persistent congestion in a feedback loop long after the trigger. This blinded monitoring and impaired EC2, Route 53, STS, and Console APIs across the region. AWS disabled the triggering activity, deployed configuration to protect the devices from congestion, and committed to fixing the back-off bug — a textbook lesson that broken retry back-off turns a transient surge into a sustained outage.

mcqs.q: What most directly characterizes a retry storm as a 'metastable' failure?
options: The system recovers automatically once the trigger ends
Retries become self-sustaining load that keeps the system overloaded even after the original trigger is gone
It only affects a single shard
It is caused purely by a hardware fault
mcqs.explanation: The hallmark is a sustained bad equilibrium: the original trigger passes, but retry traffic alone keeps offered load above capacity, so the system stays broken until load is forcibly reduced.

mcqs.q: A gateway retries 3x, the service it calls retries 3x, and that service's DB client retries 3x. In the worst case, one user request becomes how many DB calls?
mcqs.explanation: Layered retries multiply: 3 x 3 x 3 = 27. Unbudgeted retries at multiple layers amplify load catastrophically, which is why a shared retry budget across layers is essential.

mcqs.q: Clients use a fixed 1-second retry with no jitter. After a brief outage, what failure pattern emerges?
options: Retries are evenly spread, so the server absorbs them smoothly
Synchronized retry waves (thundering herd) hit the server in spikes every second
No retries occur at all
The server automatically scales to match
mcqs.explanation: Without jitter, all clients that failed together retry together, producing synchronized waves. Full jitter randomizes retry timing so the load spreads out instead of spiking.

mcqs.q: In the DynamoDB 2015 event, why did simply adding metadata capacity initially fail to resolve the outage?
options: There were no more servers available
Retry load kept the service saturated, so new capacity was immediately consumed; AWS had to pause metadata requests first
The network was still down
The fix required a region failover
mcqs.explanation: Because retries sustained the overload, added capacity was swamped on arrival. Recovery required first reducing load — pausing metadata requests to cut retries — then adding capacity and re-enabling traffic.

mcqs.q: Which combination is the most complete defense against retry storms?
options: Increase retry count and remove timeouts
Exponential backoff with full jitter, a retry budget, circuit breakers, and server-side load shedding
Retry only at the outermost layer with no limit
Disable all retries everywhere
mcqs.explanation: Backoff+jitter spreads retries, a budget caps their share of traffic, circuit breakers fail fast on unhealthy dependencies, and load shedding lets the server reject excess cheaply so it can recover. Disabling all retries sacrifices resilience to transient faults; unlimited retries cause the storm.

topics.name: Backpressure
topics.premise: The mechanism by which an overloaded consumer signals upstream producers to slow down, so the system sheds or defers load instead of collapsing. It treats overload as a normal operating mode to be detected and absorbed. Without backpressure, producers keep pushing until queues explode, latency spikes, and the service falls over.
topics.year: Borrowed from fluid/hydraulic engineering; entered computing decades ago — TCP flow control (1980s) is an early instance. Modern app-level prominence grew through the 2010s via reactive-systems / streaming frameworks (Reactive Streams, ~2013–2015). An industry/engineering term, not a single academic coining.
topics.why: Producers and consumers process at different rates. When inflow exceeds a consumer's capacity and there's no feedback signal, unbounded queues grow, memory fills, and latency degrades until failure — so the system needs an explicit signal to push the slowdown upstream.
solutions: Bounded queues / buffers
Cap in-flight work so overload becomes a fast rejection rather than an OOM crash.
Load shedding
Proactively reject a growing fraction of requests as you approach the hard limit (429/503), before latency collapses.
Rate limiting / throttling
Enforce per-principal or per-service caps (token/leaky bucket) at well-defined boundaries.
Flow-control protocols
Consumer-driven pull or credit/demand signaling (TCP windows, Reactive Streams request(n), HTTP/2 flow control).
Bulkheads
Isolate concurrency at fan-out points so one saturated dependency doesn't sink everything.
Propagate overload signals
Pass downstream 429/503 upstream so the whole call chain backs off together.
Queue-based load leveling
Buffer bursts in a queue so consumers drain at a sustainable rate.
topics.papers: No single defining paper — protocol/industry practice. Relevant: Welsh, Culler & Brewer, "SEDA", SOSP 2001 (overload control); the Reactive Streams spec (2015); Marc Brooker, "Using load shedding to avoid overload", Amazon Builders' Library.
links: Using load shedding to avoid overload — AWS
topics.takeaway: A healthy system says "slow down" — backpressure turns a catastrophic collapse into a controlled, graceful "no".
topics.deepDive:
Backpressure is the mechanism by which a downstream component signals an upstream producer to slow down when it cannot keep up. Without it, an unbounded queue absorbs the mismatch between arrival rate and service rate; the queue grows without limit, latency climbs as items wait longer, memory is exhausted, and the system eventually collapses — often taking healthy dependencies with it. Real backpressure replaces the implicit infinite buffer with an explicit bounded one and a policy for what happens when it fills: block the producer (pull/credit-based flow control, as in TCP windows or Reactive Streams request(n)), shed load by rejecting requests (HTTP 429 / 503), or drop/sample data. The core trade-off is throughput-and-completeness versus stability: blocking preserves every request but couples producer to consumer latency; shedding sacrifices some requests to keep the rest fast and the system alive.

The most dangerous failure mode is the retry storm. A slow dependency causes timeouts; clients retry; retries multiply the offered load precisely when the system has the least spare capacity; this drives latency higher, causing more timeouts and more retries — a positive feedback loop (a 'metastable failure' that persists even after the original trigger is gone). The fixes are layered: bounded queues, timeouts, exponential backoff WITH jitter (un-jittered backoff resynchronizes clients into thundering herds), retry budgets / token buckets that cap retries as a fraction of live traffic, and circuit breakers that fail fast when a dependency is unhealthy. Little's Law (L = lambda*W) is the quantitative tool: a bounded concurrency limit L caps in-flight work, so when arrival rate lambda exceeds capacity, the excess is rejected immediately rather than queued into a latency spiral.

Worked example: a service handles 1000 rps with p99 latency 50 ms, so concurrency is about 1000 x 0.05 = 50 in-flight requests. A dependency slows to 500 ms. Concurrency needed to keep 1000 rps would be 500, but the thread pool / connection pool holds only, say, 200. With an unbounded queue, requests pile up, queue wait dominates, and effective latency runs into seconds — clients time out at 1 s and retry, pushing offered load to 2000+ rps and guaranteeing collapse. With a bounded concurrency limit of 200 and a small queue, the service admits about 400 rps (200 / 0.5 s) and returns 503 for the rest immediately; callers with a retry budget back off, total load stabilizes, and the service stays up at reduced-but-predictable throughput.

Common pitfalls: unbounded queues (the default in many thread pools and message frameworks) that merely defer collapse; retries layered at every tier so a single user request fans out to N x M attempts (retry amplification); backoff without jitter; timeouts longer than the caller's own timeout (work completes after the client gave up — pure waste); and treating load shedding as 'errors' on dashboards so operators disable the very protection keeping them alive. Always shed the cheapest/lowest-priority work first and make shed responses fast and clearly distinguishable from real failures.

caseStudies.title: Amazon DynamoDB / US-East - metadata service retry storm (2015)
caseStudies.body: On September 20, 2015, a brief network blip caused many DynamoDB storage servers to re-request partition membership data from the metadata service at once. Membership payloads had grown large due to Global Secondary Indexes, so requests exceeded their time budget; servers that timed out removed themselves and retried, keeping the metadata service saturated and pushing error rates to roughly 55%. Recovery required AWS to manually pause incoming requests (apply backpressure) to shed load before they could add capacity, since the service was too overloaded to scale up. The fixes included segmenting the metadata service, adding membership-size monitoring, and reducing request rates with longer processing windows.

caseStudies.title: AWS US-EAST-1 - internal network retry congestion (2021)
caseStudies.body: On December 7, 2021, an automated scaling activity triggered unexpected behavior from a large number of clients on AWS's internal network, overwhelming the networking devices linking the internal network to the main AWS network. Increased latency and errors caused clients to make even more connection attempts and retries, and a latent bug in the clients' back-off behavior prevented them from adequately backing off, producing persistent congestion. This retry-driven feedback loop degraded EC2 control-plane APIs, STS, CloudWatch, console logins, and more for hours - a textbook absence of effective backpressure and retry control.

mcqs.q: A service's dependency slows from 50 ms to 500 ms. Clients have a 1 s timeout and retry on failure with no jitter or retry budget. The service uses an unbounded work queue. What is the most likely outcome?
options: The queue smooths the spike and latency returns to normal once the dependency recovers
A metastable retry storm: offered load multiplies, latency spirals, and the system may stay collapsed even after the dependency heals
Throughput automatically drops to match the slower dependency with no other effect
Clients silently succeed because the timeout is longer than the dependency latency
mcqs.explanation: The unbounded queue defers collapse rather than preventing it; timeouts trigger synchronized retries (no jitter) that amplify load precisely when capacity is lowest. This positive feedback loop is a metastable failure that can persist after the trigger is gone. Bounded concurrency + retry budgets + jittered backoff are the fixes.

mcqs.q: Which mechanism most directly implements backpressure rather than just masking the problem?
options: Increasing the thread pool's queue size from 1,000 to 1,000,000
A bounded concurrency limit that returns 503 immediately when in-flight work exceeds the cap
Raising the client timeout from 1 s to 30 s
Adding more retry attempts per request
mcqs.explanation: Backpressure means bounding work and signaling/rejecting excess. A bounded concurrency limit caps in-flight work (Little's Law) and sheds the rest fast. The other options enlarge the implicit buffer or amplify load, which delays or worsens collapse.

mcqs.q: Why is jitter added to exponential backoff?
options: It reduces the average wait time between retries
It encrypts the retry payload
It de-synchronizes clients so retries don't arrive as a coordinated thundering herd
It guarantees every retry eventually succeeds
mcqs.explanation: Pure exponential backoff makes many clients retry at the same instants, recreating a synchronized spike (thundering herd). Randomized jitter spreads retries over time, smoothing offered load on a recovering dependency.

mcqs.q: In the 2015 DynamoDB metadata incident, why couldn't AWS simply add capacity to recover quickly?
options: There were no spare servers available in any region
The metadata service was so overloaded by retrying storage servers that it couldn't be scaled until incoming requests were paused to shed load
A configuration file had been deleted
The outage was caused by a fat-finger command, not load
mcqs.explanation: The retry storm kept the metadata service saturated, so scaling actions couldn't take effect. AWS first applied manual backpressure (pausing requests) to relieve load, then added capacity. This shows recovery itself can require shedding load first.

mcqs.q: A request fans out: the edge retries 3x, the mid-tier retries 3x, and the data tier retries 3x. One user request can become how many backend attempts in the worst case, and what is this called?
options: 3 attempts; load shedding
9 attempts; circuit breaking
27 attempts; retry amplification
1 attempt; idempotency
mcqs.explanation: Retries multiply across tiers (3 x 3 x 3 = 27), called retry amplification. The standard mitigation is to retry at only one layer and enforce a retry budget (cap retries as a fraction of live traffic) so the system can't self-DDoS.

topics.name: Duplicate requests / idempotency gap
topics.premise: A client that doesn't get a response can't tell whether its request succeeded or failed, so it retries — and the operation may execute twice (a payment charged twice, an order placed twice). The "idempotency gap" is the window where a non-idempotent operation has no protection against being applied more than once. Because networks make at-least-once delivery the realistic default, duplicates are inevitable unless the server is designed to absorb them.
topics.year: "Idempotent" is an old mathematical term; its HTTP-method form is in the HTTP specs (RFC 2616, 1999; later RFC 7231 / RFC 9110). The practical "idempotency key" API pattern was popularized in the 2010s by payments/API companies (notably Stripe).
topics.why: Exactly-once delivery is effectively impossible over an unreliable network, so systems retry on ambiguous failures (timeouts, dropped responses). If the operation has side effects and the server treats each arrival as new, the retry causes a duplicate.
solutions: Idempotency keys
Client sends a unique key per logical operation; server stores the first result and returns the same stored response for repeats (Stripe's model).
Deduplication store
Track processed request IDs (with a TTL) and short-circuit repeats.
Idempotent API design
Prefer naturally idempotent operations (PUT/DELETE, "set to X" instead of "add X").
Conditional writes / OCC
Use version numbers or compare-and-set so a stale duplicate is rejected.
Exactly-once processing
Combine at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers (the common stream-processing pattern).
Natural unique constraints
Enforce uniqueness in the datastore (a unique order token) so a duplicate insert fails safely.
topics.papers: No single defining paper — industry practice + HTTP specs. Key: RFC 9110 "HTTP Semantics" (IETF, 2022); Stripe, "Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency" (Brandur Leach, 2017). Grounding: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications (2017).
links: Making retries safe with idempotent APIs — AWS
topics.takeaway: On an unreliable network you can't prevent duplicate requests — so design the server to make the second one a no-op.
topics.deepDive:
An idempotency gap is the window in which a retried or duplicated operation produces a duplicate side effect because the system cannot tell that it has already processed that request. It arises whenever an at-least-once delivery channel (network retries, message queues, client resubmits, timeouts that succeed server-side after the client gave up) meets a non-idempotent operation (charge a card, ship an order, increment a counter, send an email). The classic trigger: a client sends 'charge $50', the server processes it and commits, but the response is lost; the client times out and retries; without protection, the customer is charged twice. The gap exists between 'effect applied' and 'effect durably recorded as done in a way the next attempt will observe.'

The canonical fix is an idempotency key: the client generates a unique key per logical operation and sends it with every retry. The server records the key together with the result in the SAME atomic transaction as the side effect, and on a repeat key returns the stored result instead of re-executing. The subtleties are where most bugs live. (1) Atomicity: if you write the side effect and the key in separate transactions, a crash between them leaves either a duplicate (key not yet stored) or a lost result. (2) Concurrency: two retries can race in parallel before either has stored the key - you need a unique constraint, conditional write (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT, DynamoDB attribute_not_exists), or a lock so exactly one wins and the other observes the in-progress/completed state. (3) Scope and TTL: keys must be scoped to the operation and retained long enough to outlive all retries; expiring them too early reopens the gap. (4) Effects you don't control (a third-party charge API) must themselves be idempotent or wrapped so the external call is the thing keyed.

Worked example: a payment endpoint. Wrong: charge the card, then INSERT into payments. A duplicate request that arrives while the first is mid-flight (card charged, row not yet inserted) charges twice. Right: BEGIN; INSERT INTO idempotency(key) - fails on the unique constraint for a duplicate, so only one request proceeds; call the processor passing the SAME key so the processor also dedupes; store {key -> charge_id, response}; COMMIT. A retry now hits the unique constraint or finds the stored response and returns the original charge_id. Note that exactly-once delivery is impossible over an unreliable network; what you actually achieve is at-least-once delivery + idempotent processing = effectively-once effects.

Common pitfalls: relying on 'I'll just check if a row exists, then insert' (a read-then-write race - two requests both read 'absent' and both insert); using a natural key that isn't actually unique per intent (e.g., user+amount+minute collapses two legitimate identical purchases into one, an over-dedup bug); making the operation idempotent but the notification/webhook not (customer charged once but emailed twice); storing the key but committing the side effect first; and ignoring partial-failure states (request recorded as 'started' but the process crashed) so a retry sees 'in progress' forever. A robust design records explicit states (started / succeeded / failed) and makes every state transition safe to repeat.

mcqs.q: A payment service charges the card first, then INSERTs a row recording the charge in a separate step. Two retries of the same request arrive nearly simultaneously. Why can this double-charge even though it 'records' every charge?
options: Because INSERTs are always slower than card charges
Because both requests can charge the card before either has recorded the row, so neither sees the other's record (a read/write race with non-atomic effect+key)
Because the card processor caches responses for 15 minutes
Because the database lacks an index
mcqs.explanation: The side effect (charge) and the dedup record are not atomic and the check happens before the record exists. Two concurrent retries both find no prior record and both charge. The fix is to insert the idempotency key under a unique constraint in the same transaction as (or before) the effect, so exactly one request wins.

mcqs.q: Why is it impossible to guarantee true exactly-once delivery over an unreliable network, and what do we build instead?
options: It's possible with TCP; nothing extra is needed

Because acknowledgements can be lost, the sender can't distinguish 'not processed' from 'processed but ack lost'; we combine at-least-once delivery with idempotent processing to get effectively-once effects
Because clocks are never synchronized, so timestamps can't be trusted
Because encryption corrupts duplicate messages
mcqs.explanation: The two-generals problem: a lost ack is indistinguishable from a lost message, so the sender must be free to retry. Reliable systems therefore accept at-least-once delivery and make processing idempotent (via keys/dedup), yielding effectively-once side effects.

mcqs.q: A team dedups orders using the natural key (user_id, amount, item). A customer legitimately buys two identical coffees in the same minute. What bug does this cause?
options: A double charge
Over-deduplication: the second legitimate order is silently dropped because it collides with the first
A retry storm
Nothing; this is the correct design
mcqs.explanation: A natural key that isn't unique per distinct intent collapses two genuinely separate operations into one. The dedup key must represent the client's distinct logical intent (a client-generated idempotency key per request), not just the payload contents.

mcqs.q: Which property must hold for the idempotency key and the operation's side effect to close the gap reliably?
options: They must be written in two separate transactions for performance
The key must be stored and the side effect applied atomically (same transaction or equivalent), so a crash can't leave one without the other
The key must expire within one second
The key must be the user's email address
mcqs.explanation: If the effect and the key are committed separately, a crash in between yields either a duplicate (effect applied, key missing) or a lost result. Atomicity ensures a retry always observes the recorded outcome.

mcqs.q: An operation is made idempotent so the customer is charged exactly once, but they still receive two confirmation emails on a retry. What was missed?
options: The card processor is broken
Idempotency was applied to the charge but not to the downstream notification side effect; every observable side effect on the path must be deduplicated
Emails are inherently non-idempotent and cannot be fixed
The idempotency key TTL was too long
mcqs.explanation: Idempotency must cover all side effects, not just the primary one. The notification step needs its own dedup (e.g., keyed on the charge/idempotency key) so a retried request doesn't re-send the email.

topics.name: Stale cache / read-after-write inconsistency
topics.premise: When data is cached or replicated, a client can write a value and then immediately read back the old value, because the read hit a stale cache entry or a replica that hadn't received the update yet. "Read-after-write" (read-your-writes) consistency is the guarantee that you always see your own most recent write; the inconsistency is its violation — update your profile, refresh, see the old data.
topics.year: "Read-your-writes consistency" was defined among the session guarantees by Terry et al. in the Bayou project, "Session Guarantees for Weakly Consistent Replicated Data" (1994). The broader eventual-consistency framing was popularized by Amazon's Dynamo (2007) and Werner Vogels's "Eventually Consistent" (~2008).
topics.why: Reads and writes go to different places, or propagation takes time. A cache serves a value that's now outdated (no/late invalidation), or an async read replica lags the primary, so a read right after a write lands somewhere that hasn't caught up.
solutions: Cache invalidation / write-through
Invalidate or update the cache entry on write so the next read can't serve stale data.
TTL expiry
Bound staleness by expiring cache entries after a short interval (weaker but simple).
Read-your-writes routing
After a write, route that user's reads to the primary (or a replica known to have the write) for a short window.
Versioning / monotonic reads
Tag data with versions/timestamps and refuse to serve a version older than one the client already saw.
Stronger consistency where it matters
Use synchronous replication or quorum reads/writes (R + W > N) for data that can't tolerate staleness.
Cache-aside discipline
Populate cache on miss and explicitly delete-on-write to avoid serving orphaned values.
topics.papers: Terry et al., "Session Guarantees for Weakly Consistent Replicated Data", PDIS 1994. DeCandia et al., "Dynamo", SOSP 2007. Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications (2017), Ch. 5 (replication lag, read-your-writes, monotonic reads).
topics.takeaway: If your reads and writes don't go to the same place, the user will eventually see the past — invalidate aggressively or route reads to the truth.
topics.deepDive:
Stale-cache problems occur when a cache (or read replica) serves data that no longer reflects the authoritative source after a write. Caching trades freshness for latency and load reduction; staleness is the cost of that trade. The severity depends on the consistency the application needs: a product description tolerating seconds of lag is fine, but a user who just changed their password and is immediately routed to a replica that hasn't received the change (read-after-write violation) experiences a real bug. The root causes cluster into a few families: TTL-only invalidation (the cache simply waits out a timer, so writes are invisible until expiry), failed or racy invalidation (the write succeeds but the cache-delete is lost, mis-ordered, or races a concurrent read that re-populates the old value), and replication lag (a write commits on the primary but a read hits a replica that hasn't applied it yet).

The main write/cache strategies each have a distinct staleness profile. Cache-aside (lazy loading): the app reads cache, on miss loads from DB and populates; on write it updates the DB and deletes the cache entry. Its notorious race: reader A misses, reads the old DB value; before A writes it to cache, writer B updates the DB and deletes the (empty) cache; A then populates the cache with its stale read, which now persists until TTL. Write-through writes DB and cache together (fresher, but every write pays cache cost and a crash between the two writes still diverges). Write-behind/write-back buffers writes to the cache and flushes later (fast, but a crash loses buffered writes and other readers of the DB see stale data). Mitigations: delete rather than update the cache on writes (avoids storing a value computed from a soon-stale read), short TTLs as a safety net, versioned keys / generation numbers, and read-your-writes routing (pin a user to the primary or a sufficiently-caught-up replica for a window after their write).

Worked example (cache-aside race): cart count is 5, cached. User adds an item (DB -> 6) and the app deletes the cache key. But a concurrent request had already missed the cache, read 5 from the DB a moment earlier, and now writes '5' into the cache after the delete. Every subsequent reader sees 5 until the TTL expires - a lost update visible to all users. The standard fix is to bound the window (short TTL), use atomic compare-and-set on a version, or use techniques like delayed double-delete (delete cache, write DB, then delete cache again after a small delay to catch racing repopulation). For replication-lag staleness, the analogous fix is to track the write's log position and either wait for the replica to reach it or route the read to the primary.

Common pitfalls: updating the cache with the value the writer holds in memory instead of deleting (two concurrent writers leave the cache reflecting the loser); invalidating after, not as part of, the commit (a crash leaves a stale entry forever); ignoring negative caching (a cached 'not found' that outlives the row's creation); thundering herd on expiry (a hot key expires and thousands of requests stampede the DB simultaneously - mitigate with request coalescing / single-flight); and assuming a read replica is current right after a failover, when it may be hours behind. The unifying principle: decide the required consistency per read path, then choose invalidation and routing that bound staleness within that budget rather than hoping a TTL hides it.
